items.title: The Sahara was a green savannah 6,000 years ago
items.claim: Around 6,000 years ago, what is now the world's largest hot desert was something quite different. What was it?

options.text: It was already a desert; the Sahara has been arid for over 100,000 years
It was a savannah and grassland with lakes, rivers and human settlement — the 'African Humid Period'
It was a tropical rainforest like the Amazon today
It was covered by a shallow sea connected to the Mediterranean

items.reveal:
The African Humid Period lasted roughly 14,500 to 5,000 years ago. Cave paintings at Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show people herding cattle, swimming, and hunting hippos.

The cause was an orbital wobble — a stronger summer monsoon driven by changes in Earth's tilt and precession (Milankovitch cycles). When the monsoon retreated, the region desertified rapidly. Lake Chad was once larger than the Caspian Sea ('Lake Megachad').
items.why: Climate zones feel permanent on a human timescale. They are not. The Sahara's transformation in a few millennia is a reminder that 'natural' is just a snapshot of an unstable system.

items.title: Britain's climate is anomalously warm for its latitude
items.claim: London sits at 51 degrees North — the same latitude as Calgary, Canada (winters of -30 C). Why is London so much warmer?

options.text: The Gulf Stream and the wider North Atlantic Current transport tropical heat northward, with prevailing westerlies carrying it onshore
The North Sea acts as a giant heat reservoir from summer
Britain receives more solar radiation due to cloud cover patterns
The Jet Stream alone is responsible

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream originates in the Gulf of Mexico, feeds the North Atlantic Current, and as it cools and becomes saltier, sinks near Iceland and Greenland — driving the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The energy transfer is roughly 1.3 petawatts, about 10,000 times UK electricity demand.

The AMOC has weakened measurably since the mid-20th century. A collapse would cool Britain dramatically while warming the tropics — a non-linear climate flip.
items.why: Climate is not just latitude. Ocean circulation is one of the largest energy-redistribution systems on the planet, and it's not guaranteed to keep running.

items.title: The Pacific Ring of Fire produces around 90% of the world's earthquakes
items.claim: What fraction of global seismic and volcanic activity occurs around the Pacific Rim?

options.text: About 20% — earthquakes are evenly distributed globally
Around 90% of the world's earthquakes and about 75% of active volcanoes occur around the Ring of Fire, a 40,000 km horseshoe of subduction zones
About 50% of earthquakes but only 10% of volcanoes
Almost all earthquakes globally — the rest occur only in Iceland

items.reveal:
The USGS records around 90% of earthquakes (and about 80% of the largest) along the Ring of Fire. It tracks the boundaries of the Pacific Plate against the Eurasian, North American, Philippine, Cocos, Nazca and Australian plates.

Major events on the Ring include the 1960 Valdivia earthquake (Chile, magnitude 9.5 — the largest ever recorded), the 1964 Alaska earthquake (9.2), the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman (9.1) and the 2011 Tohoku event (9.0). Mount St Helens (1980), Pinatubo (1991) and Krakatoa (1883) are all Ring volcanoes.
items.why: Hazard distribution is not random. It follows tectonic structure, and the implications for hazard planning — from Tokyo's building codes to Chile's tsunami warnings — depend on understanding why.
